1937, May 12
May 12, 1937
Mr. Charles H. Chisholm 19965 Roslyn Ave., City.
My Dear Mr. Chisholm :-
God bless you. I hope you are well.
I was rather disapointed in your decision to drop my friend Garland from your employ.
I know that he liked the work and that he took an interest in it such as few of your employes are wont to take. He liked his employer and his associates. I would have been disapointed had he failed to so, because I know something of his ability.
Mr. Garland blames no one, though he was dazed at first. He is too big a character to hold petty mis- understandings, etc. He wants me to forget it as he hopes to do himself. I know that he would object to complaining to you and I am not coplaining. I am doing this without his knowledge. I am confident that you will not regret this my information, -- at least if you will have just a little patience with my effort.
I have known Mr. Garland for about ten years and I can honestly say that I doubt if I have ever met a person more solicitous to do a favor or more practical in suggesting remedies in time of difficulties. I need not go far for examples to prove this. When your Mr. Portius was in anxiety last March or early April about a very threatening difficulty, Mr. Garland had a remedy astonishingly happy in its marvelous results. Before that, when Mr. Dory and wife seemed next to desperate, and religiously paralized Garland brought them hither and they seemed to take on new life and energy. The story of Mr. J. Phillips' still in the hospital afords another example of fraternal charity, When C.H. Chisholm was threatened with blood-poison Garland
